transcript_header: Date: 2025-09-23 | Time: 16:00 UTC | Duration: 42m | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Priya (CTO, LatticeWorks), Tom (ML Eng Lead), Sara (Security), Evan (PM)
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Priya: Priya Shah here, CTO at LatticeWorks.
[00:08] Tom: Tom Alvarez, ML engineering.
[00:10] Sara: Sara Lind, security.
[00:12] Evan: Evan Park, product.
[00:14] Jordan: Great — Maya from our SE team is on as well. Maya, you want to intro?
[00:18] Maya: Yeah hi all, Maya Chen, Senior Solutions Engineer at Redwood. I'll be focused on the technical side, benchmarking and model compatibility stuff.
[00:25] Evan: Cool, high level we run customer-facing recommendation and summarization across support transcripts; we currently use OpenAI for hosted gen and a mix of vLLM for onprem experiments. We're exploring options for porting both hosted and private deployment patterns — cost/latency and eval parity are the big drivers.
[00:42] Jordan: Helpful. Can you say current traffic shape and SLOs so we can size things?
[00:46] Tom: Sure. P95 latency target for interactive features is <= 700ms for short prompts (avg 80 tokens generated); throughput for batch summarization jobs is roughly 150 concurrent requests during peak. Token volume varies — currently about 1.6M tokens/day.
[01:01] Jordan: Thanks. And what's the primary friction with your current stack? You mentioned cost and parity — any specific failures?
[01:07] Priya: Two things: first, the cost per token from our hosted provider varies and spikes for longer contexts; second, when we tried to replicate our production prompts on vLLM internally some responses diverged — the output distribution changed enough that our QA metrics dropped.
[01:24] Maya: That's the eval parity problem we see often — tokenization differences, optimizer/kernels, and sometimes decoding defaults cause drift. We have some strategies to reduce gap (prompt-normalization, reranking, quantization profiles) but it depends on model family and runtime.
[01:38] Tom: To be concrete, we tried GPT-like open models on vLLM and then swapped weights onto a TGI stack, and scores on our BLEU-like metric fell 6-9% for a subset of prompts.
[01:50] Jordan: Understood. On the product side Redwood supports hosted, Dedicated reserved pools, and Private (VPC/on-prem). For parity you'd probably want to run the same model family and tokenizer across environments and run a controlled eval — we can help orchestrate that.
[02:05] Priya: Can Redwood host Anthropic models or only open weights?
[02:09] Maya: We host a range: open weights, community-licensed models, and in some cases partner-supplied model binaries. Anthropic's commercial weights generally require licensing; for those we discuss separate arrangements. For most migrations we map to the compatible open variant or enterprise-licensed image.
[02:24] Sara: Security questions up front: we need SOC2 Type II, SSO via SAML, and customer-managed KMS for private deployments. Audit logs and retention policies too.
[02:34] Jordan: All supported. Hosted customers get SOC2 reports and fine-grain audit logs; Dedicated gives VPC egress controls and isolation; Private supports customer KMS/HSM integrations. We'll share our compliance pack.
[02:46] Sara: How about data residency? A portion of our data must stay in EU regions.
[02:50] Maya: You can pin region or run private deployment in your VPC in the EU region. For Hosted we support region routing and can restrict data to specified locations.
[02:59] Evan: On the performance side, we'd like to understand latency/cost tradeoffs. For example we saw vLLM with quantization drop latency but output quality decreased. What does Redwood recommend?
[03:10] Maya: It depends on model size and request distribution. Our Optimize tooling suggests quantization profiles per model and offers batching/caching knobs. For interactive P95 you might prefer mixed precision or 8-bit quant with a warm KV cache; for batch jobs more aggressive quant works. We'll propose per-model cost/loss curves.
[03:29] Tom: About the technical porting: we currently have TGI serving some of our smaller models and vLLM for large. We want minimal code changes — are model flavors and API compatible?
[03:39] Maya: Redwood exposes a unified REST/SDK surface. We handle kernel selection and tokenization mapping under the hood. For TGI/vLLM artifacts we often need to reserialize or convert checkpoints — sometimes tokenizers differ. We'll run a migration pass that checks tokenization and do a sample generation comparison.
[03:55] Priya: What about function calling and structured outputs? We rely on function-call-like behavior for entity extraction.
[04:00] Jordan: We support structured outputs and function-calling semantics; the SDK supports the same payloads as the hosted OpenAI-compatible flows and we can map function call metadata across model variants.
[04:12] Evan: Any quirks with streaming? We stream to the browser for interactive typing.
[04:16] Maya: Streaming supported. For Dedicated/Private the latency of first byte depends on kernel warm-up and cache; we have continuous batching and pre-warmed workers to keep first-byte low. We can instrument traces into your frontend.
[04:30] Tom: For the parity checks, what's the proposed experiment?
[04:34] Maya: Typical approach: you provide a representative prompt set (ideally 500-2k prompts across categories). We run baseline generation on your current stack and on Redwood-hosted equivalents for the same model family and decoding settings, measure your eval metrics (you pick), and identify drift. If large drift, options are: tweak tokenization, decoding (temp/top-p), or change to a different compatible checkpoint. We'll surface per-prompt regression and recommended mitigations.
[04:58] Priya: How long does a baseline run take? We want to be quick to get stakeholder buy-in.
[05:02] Maya: For 1k prompts that's usually a few hours to run end-to-end depending on sampling settings; we can parallelize. Setup time depends on private vs hosted; hosted is fastest — Dedicated/Private needs some infra prepping.
[05:15] Sara: For Private deploys — can we run air-gapped? Our compliance team asks about that for some datasets.
[05:20] Jordan: Yes — we have an on-prem package that supports air-gapped installs. It requires a slightly longer onboarding and an ops playbook but is supported.
[05:29] Evan: On pricing — are there different unit economics for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[05:33] Jordan: Hosted is consumption-based with per-token and per-embedding units; Dedicated is a reserved capacity model — you commit to a pool and get predictable throughput/lower unit cost. Private is enterprise licensing. We'll share a side-by-side and example TCO for your token volumes.
[05:48] Tom: A few more technical things: 1) How do you handle KV cache across scale-out? 2) Is there an easy way to bring our existing TGI wrappers?
[05:56] Maya: KV cache is managed per session and we support sticky routing to keep KV local; for scale-out we use sharded KV with fast transfer and cache warmers. For TGI wrappers, we usually recommend reformatting the wrapper to call Redwood SDK; we can help produce a thin adapter.
[06:13] Tom: Good. Also curious about supported quantized formats — we've been experimenting with 4-bit and 8-bit quantized checkpoints in vLLM.
[06:21] Maya: Supported — we have q4 and q8 pipelines; the performance depends on kernels available for your target GPU. If you're on Dedicated we can align instance types and kernel builds for best perf.
[06:33] Priya: Let's talk migration risk. If we onboard to Redwood and see regression we need automatic fallback to current provider during pilot. Does Redwood support fallback routing?
[06:42] Jordan: Yes — Smart routing can send traffic to alternate providers or model variants based on policy. During a pilot we often run A/B or shadow traffic and set up rollback thresholds.
[06:52] Evan: Any concerns about tokenization causing subtle semantic shifts? We had one case where different BOS/EOS handling changed summarization brevity.
[06:59] Maya: Tokenization is one of the main causes. We run token-level diffs and align tokenizers where possible; if alignment isn't perfect we use prompt normalization and small reranking model to restore behavior.
[07:13] Tom: For the benchmark, we'd like the Redwood SE to run a small sample against both vLLM and Redwood-hosted on the same hardware type if possible.
[07:21] Maya: We can mirror hardware profiles in Dedicated or run on comparable instance types in hosted. We'll document CPU/GPU types and kernel versions in the benchmark report.
[07:31] Sara: Security follow-ups: where are logs stored, and can we centrally pull audit logs? Also, can you redact PII automatically?
[07:40] Jordan: Audit logs are exportable via S3 or a SIEM connector. For PII, we have data-handling hooks and can enable redaction or tokenization pre-ingest as part of the pipeline. We'll include details in the compliance pack.
[07:54] Evan: One question around embeddings — we use embeddings for search and rerank. Do you recommend moving embeddings to Redwood as well or keep a split architecture?
[08:03] Maya: Both are common. Embeddings on Redwood gives easier co-located ops and cost visibility; some customers keep embeddings separate if they have specialized vector DB optimizations. We can show cost tradeoffs in the TCO.
[08:16] Priya: Regarding illustrations of success, what does a typical pilot look like?
[08:20] Jordan: Pilot usually: 1) scoping and prompt set, 2) baseline run + Redwood run, 3) parity analysis and tuning pass, 4) small production traffic A/B for 2-4 weeks, and 5) rollout plan for Dedicated or Private. Duration ~ 3-8 weeks depending on Private infra.
[08:38] Tom: For our team, minimal code change is a must. Can Redwood's SDK cover our existing wrapper calls?
[08:45] Maya: Yes — our SDK mirrors common shapes. We can also provide a compatibility shim for TGI-like request payloads.
[08:53] Evan: Ok that's promising. Any hidden migration costs we should budget for?
[08:58] Jordan: Mostly engineering time for prompt set curation and integration testing. Private/on-prem will add infra and ops setup. We can provide a line-item estimate in the cost sheet.
[09:08] Priya: Quick follow up: OpenAI function calling has some specialized features. If we move away, will we lose functionality?
[09:15] Maya: Redwood's function-calling is compatible in shape; certain provider-specific behaviors (e.g., proprietary heuristics) might differ. We can emulate common patterns and run functional tests as part of the parity pass.
[09:29] Tom: Let's talk about monitoring — we need token-level cost attribution and regression alerts when model output quality drops.
[09:36] Jordan: Redwood Console offers token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and eval-based quality monitoring tied to prompt sets. You can create regression alerts on your chosen metric.
[09:49] Evan: Awesome. Anything else from LatticeWorks side?
[09:52] Priya: Timeline — we want a pilot before end of Q4.
[09:55] Jordan: That's doable. We'll prioritize Hosted pilot to get fast results; if that looks good we can move to Dedicated or Private in Q1.
[10:04] Sara: Can you share a sample ISV agreement for Private deployments? Security needs to review.
[10:08] Jordan: We'll include contract templates in the follow-up packet.
[10:12] Tom: One last deep-dive question — when you say "automatic prefix/KV caching" how do you handle long conversation contexts where different shards might see different prefixes?
[10:22] Maya: We do session-aware caching; for extremely long contexts we spill to external store and stream cached KV as needed. For scale-out we rely on sticky routing plus fast cold-start transfer; the goal is to keep first-byte low while maintaining a consistent KV.
[10:40] Evan: Thanks. This has been super helpful. Can we recap action items?
[10:44] Jordan: Quick recap: Jordan to send SOC2/SAML/KMS docs and pricing; Maya to share benchmark config and vLLM/TGI compatibility notes; Tom will provide a 1k-prompt representative set; we target pilot kickoff week of 2025-10-06. Any add-ons?
[10:59] Priya: Please include the regression alerting example in the docs.
[11:03] Sara: And include retention and redaction config in the pack.
[11:07] Jordan: Noted. Anything else?
[11:09] Tom: No, that's it. Thanks everyone.
[11:12] Jordan: We'll follow up via email with the packet. Appreciate your time.
[11:17] [End of recording]

Summary: Customer (LatticeWorks) is evaluating Redwood for model portability and eval parity from current mix of OpenAI hosted and vLLM/TGI on-prem. Key concerns: latency (P95 <=700ms), cost, eval drift between runtimes, SOC2/SSO/KMS/compliance, EU data residency, and minimal code change. Redwood proposed a small pilot: 1k prompt baseline + Redwood run, parity analysis, and A/B pilot with fallback routing. Action items and timelines captured above.
